articles.title: Your Public Beta Needs a Bug Report a Stranger Can Reproduce
articles.description: Give public beta testers a short way to report what they tried, what they expected, and what...
articles.body_html:
Give public beta testers a short way to report what they tried, what they expected, and what happened. Then turn that report into a separate developer reproduction note with a known starting state, exact steps and the environment you checked. Don't make the tester do your whole debugging job.

Building in public can bring people to an unfinished product. It also creates a handoff problem: a useful comment such as “the import stopped” is not yet enough for somebody else to repeat the failure. Treat the comment as the beginning of a report, rather than proof that the reporter did something wrong.

The workflow below uses two linked records. One captures the tester's observation with little effort. The other records the developer's investigation. Keeping those jobs separate helps you preserve what was actually reported while adding the detail needed to act.

Ask for the smallest useful first report

Start with the task, the action that failed, the visible result and the expected result. Give the tester a clear route to send those details, including a private route when the information should not be public.

Ask for environment details the person can reasonably provide. “Which browser and device were you using?” is accessible. “Attach a sanitized request trace” may be too much for somebody who volunteered to try an invoice tool.

Make screenshots optional when a plain description will do. A screen can contain client names, file paths, email addresses or other information that does not belong in a public discussion. Explain what to leave out before asking for an attachment.

Don't collect every possible field just because your tracker supports it. If a version is already clear from the beta link, you can add it yourself. The first report needs enough information for the next question, not a complete diagnostic archive.

Keep the reporter's observation separate from your diagnosis

Write down what the tester saw before adding a theory about why it happened. “The spinner stayed visible after selecting Import” is an observation. “The server timed out” is a diagnosis that needs evidence.

If the reporter supplies a theory, preserve it as their suggestion. Do not silently turn it into the ticket's confirmed cause. A useful investigation can begin with an incomplete description without making the description more certain than it is.

Ask a narrow follow-up when needed. You might need to know whether the person started from a new project or reopened an existing one. That distinction is easier to answer than a general request for more information.

Keep the original report linked to your investigation note. When you later reproduce a similar symptom under different conditions, you will need to check whether you found the same problem or a different one.

Use a report format people can understand

GitHub's issue-form documentation shows examples that collect current behavior, expected behavior, reproduction steps and environment. It also supports different field types and validation. Those are tools for structuring a report, not a reason to require every field from every tester.

For a small public beta, a plain form or message can ask: what were you trying to do, where did you begin, which action changed the screen, what appeared, and what did you expect instead?

Let the person say that they do not know an answer. A guessed software version is less useful than an unknown one. You can often narrow the environment later without asking them to become familiar with your release process.

If you use a public issue tracker, say that before submission. A tester should not discover that their attachment is public only after sending it. Keep account-specific investigation in an appropriate private support route.

Build a developer note from a known starting state

Once you have the initial report, write the state needed to repeat the attempt. Include the relevant build, browser, account role and sample data. Add only details that help distinguish this attempt from a different one.

The starting state can matter as much as the clicks. An empty workspace, an existing import mapping and a previously failed upload are different conditions. If you reset the product before testing, record that reset.

Use one action per step and name the visible control. “Open a new workspace, select the sample file, then press Import” is easier to inspect than “try uploading as usual.” State the result at the step where the behavior diverges.

Keep an exact error message when it is safe to do so. Preserve relevant punctuation and wording. Remove secrets and private identifiers rather than pasting an entire log into a public ticket.

Work through a fictional CSV import failure

Imagine a fictional beta product that imports a list of workshop registrations. A tester says that importing a file stops at the mapping screen. They expected to see a confirmation showing the imported rows. This is an invented example, not a report from a real beta.

The developer asks whether the file has a header row and whether a mapping was already saved. The tester says it has a header and that they reused yesterday's workspace. The developer now has two conditions worth checking without assuming either one is the cause.

The first reproduction note uses a fresh workspace and a small invented file with name and session columns. The import succeeds. Record that result as a successful attempt under those conditions, rather than closing the original report as user error.

The next attempt starts with a saved mapping, then imports a file with one column renamed. If the failure appears there, record the exact sequence and the visible difference. You have narrowed a condition; you have not yet proved the underlying cause.

Say unreproduced when you have not reproduced it

An unreproduced report is a legitimate state. It means the investigation has not repeated the reported behavior under the conditions checked. It does not mean the person imagined it or that the product is reliable in every environment.

List the attempts that matter and the next missing detail. In the fictional example, you might still need to learn whether the original file contained an empty column. That is a concrete question the tester can answer without providing private registration data.

Avoid a long sequence of speculative requests. Each new question should help distinguish plausible conditions. If the reporter is no longer available, preserve the gap and decide what you can check independently.

When a workaround exists, describe the conditions you actually verified. “Creating a new mapping worked with our sample file” is more accurate than “just reset everything.” Be clear if the workaround would remove saved work or impose another cost.

Return a useful status to the public thread

If the report began under a public beta invitation, return with a short status that does not expose the private investigation. Say whether the issue is reproduced, still being checked, or fixed in a named available build.

Do not publish a cheerful fixed message when the change is only in a local branch. Describe the state precisely. A fix that exists but is not available to testers has not yet repaired their experience.

Invite a recheck only when the relevant version is available and participation remains optional. Give the original steps and explain which behavior should now differ. The tester should not have to rediscover the entire report to help again.

Buildside is a place for founders to share progress and questions. I founded it. A public update can explain the investigation and its limits, while the detailed report stays in the place suited to its data.

Measure the quality of the handoff

The useful question is whether another developer can reach the relevant state and inspect the claimed failure. Counted fields and long attachments cannot answer that on their own.

Before closing the ticket, ask somebody to follow the reproduction note without your verbal explanation if you have that help available. For a solo project, return to the note after a break and check which steps depended on memory.

Record what remains untested after a fix. One repaired sequence does not establish that every import combination works. Keep the scope of the public claim close to the scope of the check.

Before your next public beta invitation, try your own reporting route. Make a small invented report, turn it into a reproduction note, and identify the point where a stranger would need to ask what you meant.

articles.title: LeetCode Made Coding Fun Again
articles.description: Many of us have already fully switched to AI-powered development. We write specs, create skills,...
articles.body_html:
Many of us have already fully switched to AI-powered development. We write specs, create skills, connect MCP and run several agents in the background, after which we do a very boring code review of the result.

For almost all of this year I’ve been writing code with the help of AI, and it’s definitely productive (otherwise I wouldn’t be doing it), but it’s not as fun as it was before. Writing code is like LEGO or puzzles, first you come up with what the solution should look like, then what the first steps should be, and then you write the code, some things work right away, and some things break along the way and you rewrite what doesn’t work. And now imagine if you asked a robot to put a puzzle together for you. It’s put together, the result is there, but did you enjoy it?

I’ve heard an opinion from other developers, “Then write code without AI, what’s the problem?”, but unfortunately it’s not a solution. I think you’ve played computer games like GTA SA, where you can enter the cheat code “HESOYAM” and get a huge amount of money right away. Will you be just as motivated to earn this money in the game honestly, if you’ve used this cheat code once? Most likely not. You’ll consider it a waste of time, because you can just type a command. It’s the same with AI development. It’s very hard to make yourself sit down again and do everything by hand, when you can write a prompt and an AI agent will do it for you.

And for some time it was really sad for me. On the one hand, AI lets us be productive, make PoCs quickly and get rid of boring routine work, but on the other hand it takes away the reason why many of us fell in love with programming.

When I was just starting to learn programming in 2016-2017, I really loved challenges (I still love them, but back then it was especially important). When our C++ teacher gave us a problem on algorithms or data structures, I wanted to do it better and faster than all my classmates. It was a competition. And solving some of the problems took several days (or rather sleepless nights), for example tic-tac-toe where you play against artificial intelligence (so-called, not an LLM), or the 15 puzzle in the console.

When we finished with C++, I switched to Java/C#, where I was focused more on OOP, frameworks and patterns than on algorithms. And after that I never went back to them (except for a few tasks at work, when they really came in handy).

And now, in 2026, I’ve started solving problems on LeetCode, and it has literally taken me back to the time when it was interesting for me to write code where you had to think about algorithms, look for optimal solutions (like O(1) memory and O(n) time), and write everything yourself. Now it has become my hobby.

Some of you might think, “Why doesn’t AI get in the way of enjoying LeetCode too?” On LeetCode nobody needs the finished solution, only the process matters. Asking AI to solve a problem there is like asking a robot to put together a puzzle that you bought for fun.

I ignored LeetCode for a long time, because programming at work was enough for me. Now, when AI writes the code at work, LeetCode has become a place where I can get a challenge again.

As for the platform itself, LeetCode is not the only one you can use (it’s just one of the most popular). You can also use Codeforces, Codewars and so on.

Also, I want to mention “Advent of Code”, which is an annual event (every December) where you solve interesting programming puzzles. Here you move forward through the story and face really varied problems.

A question to my readers, how do you manage to get back the enjoyment of programming?

articles.title: How I finally understood what idempotency is
articles.description: The Intro   Idempotency. Eight letters, five syllables, and a word I pretended to understand...
articles.body_html:
The Intro

Idempotency. Eight letters, five syllables, and a word I pretended to understand in meetings for an embarrassingly long time.

It kept showing up in API docs, in Stripe's dashboard, in that one coworker's code review comments. I nodded. I did not know.

So today we are going to build the bug that makes idempotency matter, charge a fake customer twice, and then fix it. By the end, "idempotent" will be a word you can use in a sentence without sweating.

The What

Here is the dictionary version:

An operation is idempotent if performing it multiple times has the same effect as performing it once.

That's it. No, really, that's the whole concept. The hard part is noticing where it matters.

My favorite non-code example: the elevator button. Press it once, the elevator comes. Press it twelve times because you are late... the elevator still comes once. The button is idempotent. Impatient people everywhere rely on this.

Now compare that to a vending machine button. Press it twice and you get two sodas and one empty wallet. Not idempotent.

Most of your app is an elevator button. Some of it is a vending machine. The trouble starts when a vending machine gets pressed twice by accident.

The How

Let's build a tiny "pay for an order" endpoint with Express and TypeScript. One route, one fake payment provider, zero databases:

// src/server.ts
import express from 'express'

const app = express()
app.use(express.json())

const orders = new Map<string, { total: number; paid: boolean }>()
orders.set('ord_1', { total: 50, paid: false })

async function chargeCard(amount: number) {
  console.log(`💳 charged $${amount}`)
  return `ch_${Math.random().toString(36).slice(2, 8)}`
}

app.post('/orders/:id/pay', async (req, res) => {
  const order = orders.get(req.params.id)
  if (!order) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'order not found' })

  const chargeId = await chargeCard(order.total)
  order.paid = true

  res.json({ chargeId })
})

app.listen(3000, () => console.log('listening on :3000'))

Start it with npx tsx src/server.ts and pay for the order:

curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay

💳 charged $50

Lovely. Fifty bucks, one charge, everyone's happy. 🎉

Now let's be realistic about the internet. Your frontend sends the request, the server charges the card, and then... the Wi-Fi hiccups. The response never arrives. The frontend (or the HTTP client, or the user mashing the button) does what every client does when it sees a timeout: it retries.

curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay
curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay

💳 charged $50
💳 charged $50

Two charges. One order. One customer opening a support ticket with a lot of capital letters. 😬

Our endpoint is a vending machine. Every press costs money. And notice that the client did nothing wrong, retrying on a timeout is the correct thing to do. The endpoint just wasn't ready for it.

Step 1: look before you charge

The cheapest fix is to make the endpoint check its own state first:

app.post('/orders/:id/pay', async (req, res) => {
  const order = orders.get(req.params.id)
  if (!order) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'order not found' })

  if (order.paid) {
    return res.json({ chargeId: order.chargeId, alreadyPaid: true })
  }

  const chargeId = await chargeCard(order.total)
  order.paid = true
  order.chargeId = chargeId

  res.json({ chargeId })
})

(Add chargeId?: string to the order type so TypeScript stops yelling.)

Run the double curl again:

💳 charged $50

One charge. The second request got a polite "yep, already done" with the same chargeId as the first. Press the elevator button all you want now.

That's idempotency in one if. The operation "pay order 1" now has the same result whether you call it once or five hundred times.

Step 2: the sneaky gap

Before you ship, let's be honest about a hole. What if the two requests arrive at the same time? Both read paid === false, both charge, both set paid = true. Our if didn't help.

In a real app with a real database you close that gap by making the "check and mark" step atomic. In Postgres that's something like:

UPDATE orders SET paid = true WHERE id = $1 AND paid = false

If that update touches one row, you won the race, go charge the card. If it touches zero rows, someone else got there first, return their result. Same idea as our if, just one that the database enforces so two requests can't both pass.

Step 3: idempotency keys (the grown-up version)

There's one more case the paid flag can't cover: what if the client legitimately wants to pay twice? Say, two different orders that happen to look identical, or a "buy again" button.

The industry answer is an idempotency key. The client generates a random ID per attempt and sends it in a header. The server remembers which keys it has seen:

const seen = new Map<string, unknown>()

app.post('/orders/:id/pay', async (req, res) => {
  const key = req.header('Idempotency-Key')
  if (!key) return res.status(400).json({ error: 'Idempotency-Key header required' })

  if (seen.has(key)) {
    return res.json(seen.get(key))
  }

  const order = orders.get(req.params.id)
  if (!order) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'order not found' })

  const chargeId = await chargeCard(order.total)
  order.paid = true

  const response = { chargeId }
  seen.set(key, response)
  res.json(response)
})

curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123"
curl -X POST localhost:3000/orders/ord_1/pay -H "Idempotency-Key: abc-123"

💳 charged $50

Same key, one charge, identical response both times. A retry is now safe by design: the client keeps the same key while retrying, and only generates a new one when it genuinely wants a new action.

This is exactly what Stripe, PayPal and friends ask you to send. Now you know why. 🧠

(In production, seen lives in your database or Redis with an expiry, not in a Map. But the shape is the same.)

Step 4: wait, we trust the client to pick the key?

Yep. And it has to be that way. Look at it from the server's side: two identical POST /orders/ord_1/pay requests show up. Is that a flaky network resending one payment, or a customer who genuinely wants to buy twice? The server has no idea. Only the thing that decided to pay knows if it's deciding again. So the client tags the decision, and retries carry the same tag.

What we don't do is trust the client blindly. The server adds a few guardrails:

  • Scope the key to the user. Look it up as (userId, key), not just key. Nobody can replay or collide with someone else's request.
  • Fingerprint the body. Store a hash of the request along with the key. Same key, different body? That's not a retry, that's someone being clever. Answer with a 422.
  • Expire keys. Keep them for a day or so, then forget them. A retry from last month is not a retry.
  • Lock while in flight. If a second request with the same key arrives while the first is still running, make it wait (or return a 409). That also closes the race from Step 2.

With those four, the client can only ever use a key to say "that same thing again, please". Which is exactly what we wanted.

The Why

Let's zoom out, because this is bigger than payments:

  • Retries are everywhere. HTTP clients retry. Message queues redeliver. Users double-click. Cron jobs overlap. If your operation isn't idempotent, every one of those is a bug waiting for a bad Wi-Fi day.
  • Idempotent code is restartable code. A script that imports 10,000 rows and crashes at row 7,000? If each row is an "insert or update", you just run it again. If it's "insert", you now have 7,000 duplicates and a long afternoon.
  • HTTP already has opinions. GET, PUT and DELETE are supposed to be idempotent. POST is not. That's why "create order" is a POST and "set order status" is a PUT. Delete something twice and the second call should say "fine, it's gone" rather than crash.
  • It's a design question, not a library. No package makes your code idempotent. You get it by asking, for every action: "what happens if this runs twice?" and making the answer "nothing new".

The one-sentence version to keep in your pocket: pressing it again should never make things worse.

The Goodbye

Next time someone drops "we should make that idempotent" in a review, you can nod and know. Even better, you can go find the endpoint in your app that charges, emails or creates something, run it twice, and see what happens.

Go press some elevator buttons. Happy coding 🤝

articles.title: API key security after the OpenCode Console breach
articles.description: API key security after OpenCode's reported Console breach: affected scope, hosted provider credentials, practical checks and the limits of the public notice.
articles.body_html:
OpenCode reports a security breach affecting 1.4% of its Console users, specifically a subset with external providers linked. The latest edited notice says those users were emailed and the incident is ongoing. For API key security, the useful first question is which component holds the credential. A familiar product name can hide several different answers.

TL;DR

  • The reported percentage is of Console users. Installing the local OpenCode agent alone does not establish inclusion in the affected group.
  • Console's documentation says it stores connected provider credentials and serves requests through a shared gateway. That is the documented architecture; the incident's access path remains undisclosed.
  • Review the official notification and provider activity. Preserving evidence, revoking suspicious credentials and updating affected integrations are general incident-hygiene advice.
  • “Distillation” describes an alleged purpose involving model outputs. The public notice leaves the attacker identity, full customer impact and completed fix open.
  • Sphinx and Pele, two other fresh developer tools, have useful documented boundaries of their own. Read those before adopting either one.

OpenCode Console breach: what the statement actually establishes

The original announcement linked from Hacker News has a newer edited version. The newer statement matters because it spells out a condition that changes how a reader interprets the incident: the affected users had external providers linked. The same statement says OpenCode notified them by email and that users who did not receive an email were not impacted. That is the company's current affected-user claim. It should remain attributed to the company when repeated.

The 1.4% figure needs its denominator attached every time. The population is Console users. The notice does not supply the population's size, so it does not support an absolute victim count. It also does not support applying the percentage to all OpenCode installations, monthly users or GitHub followers. Multiplying two unrelated marketing numbers would make an impressive graphic and an inaccurate one.

The public statement says the team is working with Anthropic, OpenAI and Google to remediate. It says details cannot be shared yet because the incident is ongoing. Those are response statements. They leave several ordinary incident questions unanswered: how access was gained, what exact credential handling failed, how much unauthorized activity occurred and which changes will prevent a recurrence.

Individual replies about missing credit or unexpected usage deserve investigation. This article does not independently verify those reports, turn them into a loss total or promise reimbursement. There is no verified reimbursement commitment in the cited notice. A screenshot of somebody's bill would still need an account of what caused the change before it became an incident-wide fact.

We covered the initial announcement as an overnight side story in the previous episode. This is an explicitly requested follow-up, with more room for the scope and documented architecture. My earlier NEEDS REVIEW verdict remains a useful starting position while the technical report is missing.

API key security starts with a credential map

OpenCode's product page describes an open-source coding agent for the terminal, editor and desktop. The Console model documentation describes an optional provider that can be used with OpenCode or another coding agent. A person may use OpenCode with a different provider arrangement. The local agent's name therefore cannot establish whether the person used the affected hosted service.

The Console provider documentation supplies a concrete architectural fact: Console stores a connected provider credential and serves that provider through its gateway. Workspace members can use the models without seeing the upstream provider key. Owners and administrators manage these connections through the Providers tab.

That arrangement has an obvious administrative benefit. A team can share model access without copying an upstream key to every member. It also gives the gateway responsibility for a credential that unlocks an external service. The documented convenience and the documented trust boundary are part of the same design.

A useful inventory separates the pieces:

Piece Question to answer
Local coding agent Which provider configuration does this agent use?
Hosted Console workspace Which external accounts have been connected here?
Provider credential Who can revoke it and where can its activity be inspected?
Downstream integration Which tools depend on this credential being valid?

This is an inventory template. It is not a reconstruction of the attack. Drawing an attacker moving along these boxes would imply knowledge the announcement has not supplied. The exact failure could involve a different part of the service, and the eventual report will have to explain that.

For the same reason, keeping the percentage narrow does not make the impact trivial. A subset can contain people with serious exposure. Scope helps those people find the right response and helps other readers avoid treating an unrelated component as a confirmed victim.

What to check when provider credentials may be exposed

Start with the official notice and your own account arrangement. Establish whether external providers were connected through Console. Review the notification the company says it sent. If something about your account remains unclear, use the official support channel and ask about that concrete configuration rather than trying to diagnose it from another person's reply thread.

Then review provider activity. Preserve the relevant timestamps and records before changing the credential arrangement, where that is practical and consistent with containing suspicious use. If you identify suspicious activity, revoke the exposed credential through the provider that issued it. Update affected integrations with a deliberate replacement rather than leaving a silently failing tool in the background.

These are general incident-response habits, offered as editorial advice. OpenCode's announcement has not published a complete customer remediation checklist. Follow any newer, account-specific instructions that the company and the affected provider supply. The live notice should be rechecked before this piece is published because an ongoing incident can change while a video is being edited.

For future integrations, record where a credential lives, which upstream account it reaches and who owns revocation. Restrict its permissions and spending where the provider supports that. Review activity and keep an inventory of dependencies that will need updating after a replacement. The exact controls depend on the provider and account type; a generic “rotate everything” slogan does not perform that inventory for you.

I would also distinguish the service's access controls from the agent's working permissions. A code-review hook, terminal prompt or confident model answer supplies a different kind of assurance. It does not establish the security of a hosted credential store. Developers already spend enough time asking whether a green badge means what they think it means.

What “distillation attack” tells us

Anthropic's background explanation defines distillation as training a less capable model on the outputs of a stronger one. The technique also has legitimate uses. A provider can distill its own models into smaller versions; unauthorized extraction campaigns use outputs for a different purpose.

OpenCode associates this breach with a large-scale distillation attack. The useful reading is that this describes the alleged purpose of the activity. It leaves the access mechanism open. The words do not identify an attacker, explain how credentials were handled or quantify what happened to customers.

Anthropic's February article discusses separate cases. Its named organizations and account totals must stay attached to those cases. They provide no attribution for this OpenCode incident. A story can have a plausible motive while still lacking a public technical cause, and the two should remain separate fields in the reporting.

The later report should help customers answer what changed in the system they actually used. Until then, an elaborate attack diagram would mainly demonstrate how well the illustrator can connect arrows.

Also today: Sphinx asks you to explain the diff

Sphinx is a Git hook that pauses protected-branch pushes for an understanding check. A separate reviewer reads the committed change without the generating chat. It asks about behavior and failure cases. Its published worker/redelivery conversation is illustrative; we have not installed Sphinx or measured a production-review improvement.

The adoption caveats deserve attention. Installation changes the global Git hook path. The reviewer provider receives changed code and answers. Filename-based exclusions cannot catch a secret embedded in ordinary source. There is no default cap on model calls; a typical check uses five to eight requests plus about one per answer. Local hooks can be bypassed, and the examiner can be wrong. This is an exercise in understanding with costs and data flow to inspect.

Also today: Pele changes the theme while keeping the SVG

Obsidian's kepano released Pele, a Mermaid-to-SVG renderer with CSS-variable theming. Its bundle table reports about 230 kB compressed against Mermaid's 1.6 MB. Speed comparisons remain the project's measurements; we did not reproduce them.

We did make a small behavior check in the real homepage editor. Changing the documented CSS variables preserved the same SVG node and four labels while the computed background and line colors changed. That demonstrates the advertised theme behavior, with no claim about render speed.

The security page says displayed images can make network requests, and the application owns supplied icon markup and internal-link navigation. Links and images can be disabled. Source/output limits are documented. A smaller dependency still arrives with responsibilities for its caller.

Verdict: NEEDS REVIEW

I'd keep the Console incident under review until enough information is published to assess the affected credentials and the fix. The practical habit is to identify which service actually holds your provider access. That information remains useful after the current headline leaves the front page.

FAQ

Does using the local OpenCode agent put me in the reported affected group?

Installation alone does not establish that. The official notice names a subset of Console users with external providers linked. Check your own provider arrangement and the company's notification.

Does 1.4% tell us how many people were affected?

The total Console population is undisclosed in the cited notice. An absolute count cannot be calculated from that statement alone.

Has OpenCode published the root cause or completed fix?

The reviewed notice says the incident is ongoing and additional details cannot yet be shared. It states that the team is working with three providers to remediate. It does not establish completion.

Will an AI understanding check secure my provider credentials?

A tool such as Sphinx asks a different question: whether you can explain a committed change. Its own documentation exposes reviewer limitations and data flow. Credential storage needs its own reviewed controls.

Sources

  • Latest edited OpenCode notice
  • OpenCode product
  • Console provider gateway
  • Optional Console models
  • Distillation background
  • Sphinx documentation
  • Pele
  • Pele security
  • Pele maintainer explanation

articles.title: My AI Experiment Was Going Great Until My Client Replied 😂
articles.description: Quick confession. Last Sunday I opened dev.to and my brain made a tiny error noise. 😵  Opus against...
articles.body_html:
Quick confession. Last Sunday I opened dev.to and my brain made a tiny error noise. 😵

Opus against GPT-6 against Gemini 4. One post said Gemini wins twelve of eighteen benchmarks. Another said a Meta model costs the same as Opus and loses most of its own tests. One minute of scrolling. Zero joy.

So I made a deal with myself. Thirty days. One editor, VS Code. One model, Claude Sonnet 5.5, on the free plan. Yes, free. 😂 Every new launch was allowed to happen without me.

My old routine, for context. Google AI Studio on Monday, trying one Gemini flavour after another. DeepSeek on Tuesday because a bug felt like its kind of bug. Then I'd test a few models inside my AI powered projects too. I called it research. My calendar called it wandering. 🧭

That same week, FrancisTRdev's ( @francistrdev ) post about AI fatigue was sitting in my feed. He misses the dev.to from before 2022, the one with CSS tips and small weird projects, and he hopes AI becomes a quiet boring tool in the toolbox. Boring! That's the exact word I wanted for my editor. His post got well over a hundred reactions, so I'm clearly not the only tired one.

Sylwia Laskowska ( @sylwia-lask ) wrote about AI features that run in the browser and what your hardware can really handle. Jamilxt ( @jamilxt ) keeps pointing out that a model priced at two dollars per million tokens can still give you a very different real bill. 💸 Maame Afua A. P. Fordjour ( @maame-codes ) wrote that localhost is a lie, because real users break clean databases. Three different voices, one message. Real work beats shiny news.

So what did my thirty days look like?

Quiet. Busy, but quiet. I finished a few client projects, some for clients in India, many of them ecommerce sites. I built the website for my agency TheBitForge ( @thebitforge ) and worked on its projects. I wrote a few articles for topblogs.online and some other places. And after a few emails with the founder of Floot.com, I used a paid Floot plan connected with Claude to build a full stack blogging platform with an admin panel and AI summaries for every article, plus a newsletter system for my own use.

Claude Sonnet 5.5 helped me well through all of it, the ecommerce work included. And look at that list again. Where's the new model? Nowhere. I just finished things.

Now the part that hurt.

One client got their ecommerce website from me. They didn't like it. A few days later they came back and asked me to redesign the whole thing again. All of it. 😅

That was easily the worst moment of my month. And here's the strange part. No model on earth could have stopped it. Not the newest one, not the priciest one, not the one with twelve benchmark wins. A client's taste isn't inside any benchmark. Maame was right. The hard part of this job is people, not tokens.

What I'm taking from it? Show the client a rough version sooner, before the pretty one. Ask what they hate before I build anything. Simple, a bit embarrassing that I needed a full redesign to learn it. 🙃

Do I think everyone should stay on one model? No. If your job is literally comparing models, please keep comparing. For the rest of us, I'd check the news once a month instead of once an hour. If something is truly better, it'll still be better in four weeks, and by then someone on dev.to has probably tested it and posted the real bill.

Your turn. Has a client ever asked for a full redesign right after you delivered? How did you handle it? And which model are you on right now? Tell me below, I'm genuinely curious. 👇

articles.title: OpenPilot vs Cursor, Cline and Continue: an honest comparison (from the person who built OpenPilot)
articles.description: I'm the solo dev behind OpenPilot, an open-source desktop agent that runs on whatever model you give...
articles.body_html:
I'm the solo dev behind OpenPilot, an open-source desktop agent that runs on whatever model you give it. People keep asking how it compares to Cursor, Cline and Continue, so here's my best attempt at a fair answer. I'm obviously biased, so I've stuck to things you can check in each project's own docs or code, and I've linked them. Where another tool is better, I say so.

Everything below was checked on October 17, 2026. These tools change fast, so if something is out of date, tell me in the comments and I'll fix it.

The short version

  • Cursor is the most polished experience: a full editor with Tab completion, cloud agents and its own models. It's proprietary, and on the Free and Plus plans you can't use your own API keys or third-party models.
  • Cline is the most capable open-source option. It's Apache-2.0 and ships as a VS Code extension, a JetBrains plugin, a CLI and an early desktop app. It works with basically any provider, including Ollama and LM Studio. If you want open source and maximum features, start there.
  • Continue was a pioneering open-source assistant, but its repo is now read-only and no longer actively maintained, after a final 2.0.0 release.
  • OpenPilot is a small, chat-first desktop app (MIT, Electron). You point it at a folder, bring any OpenAI-compatible model, and approve what it runs. It's simpler and much younger than the others, and it's a one-person project.

Side by side

Cursor Cline Continue OpenPilot
License Proprietary Apache-2.0 (JetBrains plugin not open-sourced) Apache-2.0 MIT
Form factor Full editor VS Code ext, JetBrains plugin, CLI, desktop app (v0.0.x), SDK VS Code ext, JetBrains plugin, CLI Standalone desktop app (Electron)
Bring your own key Yes, on Premium and above (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Azure, Bedrock); not on Free/Plus Yes Yes Yes, it's the only way it works
Local models (Ollama / LM Studio) Not among the documented BYOK providers Yes Yes Yes (Ollama preset; LM Studio via custom base URL)
Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint Not documented for BYOK Yes Yes Yes
Approval before commands/edits Has agent review and security settings (see their docs) Yes, every edit and command by default, with auto-approve available — Yes for shell commands, file writes and edits: Deny / Allow / Allow all for this session
Undo / checkpoints — Yes (checkpoints) — No. Use git
Tab autocomplete Yes (Cursor's own models, even with BYOK) — Yes No
MCP Yes Yes Yes Yes
Maintained Yes Yes, very active No, read-only repo Yes (solo)
Price Free tier, paid from $8/mo Free (you pay your model provider) Free Free (you pay your model provider, or nothing with local models)

Sources: Cursor BYOK docs, Cursor plans, Cline README, Continue README and docs, OpenPilot source.

A "—" means I couldn't confirm it from official docs. Please don't read it as "no".

Cursor

Cursor is a full editor, and it's genuinely good at being one: Tab completion, Plan Mode, cloud agents, code review and a long list of integrations. Its BYOK docs are clear about the trade-offs.

  • Supported key providers are OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Azure OpenAI and AWS Bedrock.
  • Custom keys only work for chat models. Tab keeps using Cursor's built-in models.
  • Requests are routed through Cursor's servers for final prompt building, even with your own key. Cursor says the key isn't stored.
  • On the current plans table, Free and Plus don't include third-party models or your own API keys. Premium ($30/mo) and up do.

If you're happy inside Cursor and paying for a plan that fits, I honestly don't think you need OpenPilot. Where it's a poor fit is if you want to run a model on your own machine, use a provider that isn't on that list, or keep requests from passing through a third-party backend.

Cline

Cline is what I'd recommend to most people asking for "open-source Cursor". It runs in VS Code and JetBrains, as a CLI (npm i -g cline), and now as a desktop app. Its features include:

  • Plan and Act modes
  • Checkpoints, so you can undo the agent's work
  • Diffs you can review
  • Linter and compiler awareness
  • Rules and skills, MCP and plugins
  • Multi-agent teams and scheduled agents
  • A huge provider list: Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, OpenRouter, Bedrock, Vertex, Groq, Ollama, LM Studio and any OpenAI-compatible API

By default it asks before every file edit and terminal command, and you can switch on auto-approve.

Compared with that, OpenPilot is a much smaller tool. Cline's desktop app is newer (v0.0.x at the time of writing), but the project overall is far more mature than mine.

Continue

Continue deserves credit for pushing open-source, any-model coding assistants early. As of now, its README says the continuedev/continue repository is no longer actively maintained and is read-only. The team shipped a final 2.0.0 of the VS Code extension, CLI and JetBrains plugin, and that release also removed anonymous telemetry. You can still install it, but don't expect fixes.

OpenPilot: what it actually is

I built OpenPilot because I wanted a Cursor-style agent where I pick the model, including local ones, without living inside a particular editor. In practice:

  • It's a desktop chat app. You add one or more models with a name, a base URL and a key. There are presets for OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenRouter, DeepSeek, Groq, Together, Mistral, xAI, MiniMax and Ollama, or you can use any custom OpenAI-compatible URL. You can switch models per chat.
  • You pick a workspace folder. The agent can list, read, write and edit files there, and edits show a diff preview. It can also run shell commands (output streams into the chat), plan with a todo list, and hand side tasks to short-lived subagents.
  • Shell commands, file writes and file edits pause on an Allow / Deny card unless you turn on "Enable all permissions" in Settings → Agent, which is off by default. I wrote up how that loop works, and where it doesn't protect you, in a separate post.
  • MCP servers can be turned on per chat. It also has skills (type /), persistent memory, token usage by model, and optional web search through TinyFish.
  • Keys stay on your machine. There's no account.

Honest limits:

  • It's a solo project at v1.0.5.
  • The Windows installer is unsigned, so SmartScreen will warn you. macOS is an unsigned beta, and on Linux you build from source.
  • There's no checkpoint or undo. Work in a git repo.
  • There's no Tab autocomplete, and it isn't an editor. I use it next to one.
  • Small local models (I've tested Qwen 3 8B and 27B) do fine on focused edits but get lost on long multi-step tasks. There's no loop guard yet.
  • Anonymous usage telemetry (app opens, feature and model use, token counts; no chats, files, paths or keys) is on by default. You can turn it off in onboarding or Settings → About.

So which one?

  • You want the best editor experience and you're fine paying: Cursor.
  • You want open source with the most features, inside your editor or CLI: Cline.
  • You want a small, standalone open-source app where any OpenAI-compatible or local model drives an agent in a folder, and you approve each command: try OpenPilot, and tell me what breaks.

Links: GitHub · openpilot.in · Run it with Ollama + Qwen 3 · Run it with LM Studio

Disclosure: I drafted this post with help from an AI assistant and checked the claims against each project's docs and source on Oct 17, 2026. If I got something wrong about any of these tools, please correct me in the comments and I'll update it.

articles.title: Exact-Match Edits vs Patches: How Claude Code, Codex and Aider Write to Your Files
articles.description: Claude Code's Edit refuses a duplicate match; Codex's apply_patch and Aider's SEARCH/REPLACE take the first one. How each edit protocol fails.
articles.body_html:
• Book: Prompt Engineering Pocket Guide
  • Also by me: Thinking in Go (2-book series) — Complete Guide to Go Programming + Hexagonal Architecture in Go
  • My project: Hermes IDE | GitHub — an IDE for developers who ship with Claude Code and other AI coding tools
  • Me: xgabriel.com | GitHub

Your config file has two functions that both set timeout = 30. You ask a coding agent to raise the production timeout to 60. Depending on which agent you asked, one of two things happens. The edit is refused until the agent adds more context. Or the first timeout = 30 in the file changes, which is the development one, and the patch applies cleanly.

The edit protocol decides that outcome: the format the agent uses to describe a change, and the code on your machine that applies it. Claude Code, Codex and Aider each use a different one, and their docs and source say exactly what happens when the text doesn't line up.

Here is the file used for every case below:

def load_dev():
    timeout = 30
    retries = 3

def load_prod():
    timeout = 30
    retries = 5

Three ways to say "change this line"

Claude Code: exact string replacement. The Edit tool takes an old_string and a new_string and, in the docs' words, "doesn't use regex or fuzzy matching." Three checks must pass: Claude has read the file, old_string appears exactly as written, and it appears exactly once unless replace_all: true is set. The read rule is looser for newer models. The same page says Claude Opus 4.6, Claude Haiku 4.5 and older models always require the read, while newer models on Claude Code v2.1.208 or later can skip it when the Read tool is available and reading wouldn't need a permission prompt.

The documented fields, for our task:

Edit
  old_string: "    timeout = 30"
  new_string: "    timeout = 60"
  replace_all: false

Codex: patch envelopes. OpenAI's Codex Prompting Guide tells you to use apply_patch for single-file edits, says the model "has been trained to excel at this diff format", and strongly recommends using OpenAI's exact implementation. That implementation is open source in the codex-rs/apply-patch crate. Its markers are *** Begin Patch, *** Add File:, *** Delete File:, *** Update File:, *** Move to:, *** End of File, @@ and *** End Patch. Changed lines start with - or +, context lines with a space, and there are no line numbers:

*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: config.py
@@
-    timeout = 30
+    timeout = 60
*** End Patch

Aider: you pick the format. Aider's edit formats include whole (the model returns the entire file), diff (SEARCH/REPLACE blocks), diff-fenced (the same blocks with the path inside the fence, mainly for Gemini models), udiff (a simplified unified diff) and two editor- variants for architect mode. A diff block looks like a merge conflict:

config.py
```python
<<<<<<< SEARCH
    timeout = 30
=======
    timeout = 60
>>>>>>> REPLACE
```

Aider also publishes how often models get the format right. Its polyglot leaderboard, last updated November 20, 2025, puts a "Correct edit format" column next to the pass rate over 225 exercises. gpt-5 (high) tops the table at 88.0% correct, with 91.6% on edit format using diff. Even the top model sent a malformed edit in some cases, and the applier has to catch each one.

The duplicate line: one refuses, two pick the first

Claude Code's uniqueness check fails, because timeout = 30 appears twice. Per the docs, Claude then "either supplies a longer string with enough surrounding context to pin down one occurrence, or sets replace_all: true to replace them all." The retry that works carries the function header:

Edit
  old_string: "def load_prod():\n    timeout = 30"
  new_string: "def load_prod():\n    timeout = 60"
  replace_all: false

Codex's applier doesn't check uniqueness. In file_update.rs, each chunk's old lines are searched from the current position forward, and seek_sequence.rs returns the first window that matches without looking at later ones. With the bare @@ patch above, the first timeout = 30 sits in load_dev. That line changes.

The anchor fixes it. Text after @@ is a change context: the applier finds that line first and only searches for the old lines after it.

*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: config.py
@@ def load_prod():
-    timeout = 30
+    timeout = 60
*** End Patch

Aider's diff format behaves like Codex here. In editblock_coder.py, perfect_replace replaces the first block of lines that matches and returns. One path is stricter. When a SEARCH block uses ... to elide lines, Aider refuses the block if that chunk appears more than once.

To be fair to Codex and Aider, models rarely send one bare line. Context lines in a patch and a multi-line SEARCH block usually make the match unique anyway. The difference shows up when they don't: Claude Code stops, the other two apply at the first match.

Stale context: the file moved since the model looked

The model's copy of a file goes stale when you edit it, a formatter runs, or a second agent touches it.

Claude Code has a documented rule for this case. Since v2.1.208, if the file changed after Claude's last read but old_string still matches the current content "exactly and unambiguously" and the file is readable without a prompt, the edit applies and the result notes that the file carries other changes, so Claude re-reads before edits that depend on the surrounding code. In any other case, such as a stale old_string, Claude reads the file again before editing. Before v2.1.208 it refused any edit to a file that changed on disk after the read.

Codex fails with a message the model can act on. If the @@ line isn't found, file_update.rs returns Failed to find context '<line>' in <path>. If the old lines aren't found, it returns Failed to find expected lines in <path>: followed by the lines it looked for. The API guide describes the same loop for your own harness: report status: "failed" with a short human-readable message.

Aider replies with SearchReplaceNoExactMatch: This SEARCH block failed to exactly match lines in <path>, plus the reminder that "The SEARCH section must exactly match an existing block of lines including all white space, comments, indentation, docstrings, etc". If misses keep coming, its troubleshooting page suggests, among other things, --edit-format whole.

The whole format can't miss a match, because there is nothing to match. If the model's copy of the file was old, though, the rewrite puts that old version back over whatever changed since, and nothing reports an error. The other risk is elision. The edit-formats page says udiff was mainly used with GPT-4 Turbo because it reduced that model's habit of eliding code with comments like "original code here". In Aider's unified diffs write-up, moving GPT-4 Turbo from SEARCH/REPLACE to udiff raised its laziness benchmark score from 20% to 61%.

Whitespace drift: strict, forgiving, and in between

Models re-type the text they want to replace, and re-typing drifts. A tab comes back as four spaces, trailing whitespace disappears, a straight quote turns curly.

Claude Code is strict on purpose. The docs say "A single character of whitespace or indentation difference is enough to miss." When it misses, the edit doesn't apply.

Codex's applier is the most forgiving of the three. seek_sequence makes four passes in what its comment calls "decreasing strictness": an exact match, then ignoring trailing whitespace, then trimming both sides, then normalising common Unicode punctuation like dashes and quotes to ASCII. Indentation drift in the old lines still finds its target. The price shows up when nothing matches exactly. A looser pass can match in more places, and the first window it finds wins.

Aider sits in between. It tries an exact match, then a match that tolerates missing leading whitespace, then retries without a stray blank first line. A fuzzy edit-distance matcher exists in the same file, but a bare return sits in front of the call, so it never runs.

Leniency pays off. The same unified diffs write-up reports that turning flexible patching off produced "a 9X increase in editing errors".

Failure Claude Code Edit Codex apply_patch Aider diff
Duplicate match Refused First match after anchor First match
Stale text Applies if still exact, else re-reads Error to model Error to model
Whitespace drift Miss Four lenient passes Tolerates leading whitespace

An undo that doesn't care how the bytes got there

Every failure above has a quiet version: the edit applies in the wrong place, or on top of stale assumptions, and the agent reports success. You catch it in review, and then you want that one turn back.

Each tool has its own answer. Claude Code's checkpoints capture your code before each prompt, and /rewind restores code, conversation or both. The docs are clear about the edge: "Checkpointing does not track files modified by Bash commands", and most subagent edits aren't restored either. Aider commits every edit to git with a descriptive message, and /undo discards the last change. Each one covers its own agent's edits and nothing else.

I build Hermes IDE, so weigh this with that in mind. Hermes runs Claude Code, Codex, Aider and other agents, each in its own terminal, and saves every agent turn, so you can diff or restore any single turn, with undo (README). The strip under a session lists the agent's replies with the lines each changed. Click one to see its changes or restore your files to that point (2.3.1 notes). The Review Desk (⌘G) shows the same work by turn or by file.


The Review Desk (⌘G) in By turn view for a Claude Code task: two turns, turn 1's diff of src/db.ts, the changed files, and a commit message drafted from the turns.

Because the snapshot is of your files, not of the edit calls, the same restore works for every agent, whether the change arrived as an old_string, a patch envelope or a SEARCH block. There are two limits. In a Claude Code task with extra folders, the strip tracks the main project only (2.3.1 notes). Turn snapshots from tasks that ran in their own worktree are removed 14 days after the session closes (2.2.9 notes).

What to do with this

If you run Codex or Aider on files with repeated blocks, like per-environment config or test tables, check where the diff landed, not only what it says.

If Claude Code keeps missing an edit, look for mixed tabs and spaces or invisible characters in the file before you blame the model. If you use Aider's whole format, keep other writers off that file while the agent works, because a rewrite from a stale copy applies without an error.

Whatever the protocol, keep a per-turn record outside the edit path: plain commits, Aider's auto-commit, or a turn snapshot.

If this was useful

An edit format is structured output with a strict parser on the other end, and Aider's leaderboard shows that even top models miss the format in some share of cases. If you write prompts that ask a model for output a program has to parse, the Prompt Engineering Pocket Guide is my short book on prompting techniques, structured output among them. If you run several of these agents side by side, Hermes IDE is free to download, source-available under BSL 1.1, runs on macOS, Windows and Linux, and lives on GitHub.

articles.title: The Lock Type Didn't Make My Locks Faster
articles.description: A reviewer told me to swap lock(object) for the new System.Threading.Lock type for the speed. I benchmarked it on .NET 10 and the stopwatch had other ideas.
articles.body_html:
A reviewer left one comment on my PR: "swap these lock(_gate) to the new Lock type, it's faster." I'd been meaning to try System.Threading.Lock anyway, and "faster" is the kind of word that gets me to actually do a thing. So I expected to come back with a nice before/after number, paste it in the thread, and feel clever. That's not what the stopwatch said.

Quick refresher on what the type even is. Since .NET 9 there's a real System.Threading.Lock class, and in C# 13 the lock statement knows about it. When you write lock(x) and x is a Lock, the compiler stops emitting Monitor.Enter/Monitor.Exit and lowers it to x.EnterScope() instead, which returns a disposable scope. Same keyword you've typed a thousand times, different machinery underneath. The pitch is a leaner lock that doesn't lean on the object header the way monitors do.

What I measured

I wanted the simplest honest question first: single thread, no contention, how long does it take to just grab and release the lock 50 million times while bumping a counter. Uncontended acquire/release is the path that runs on every lock you've ever written, contended or not, so if there's a cheap win hiding anywhere it should show up here.

object _objectGate = new();
Lock _lockGate = new();

// A: the classic, Monitor under the hood
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    lock (_objectGate) { c++; }

// B: same keyword, Lock type -> compiler calls EnterScope()
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    lock (_lockGate) { c++; }

// C: the explicit form B lowers to
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    using (_lockGate.EnterScope()) { c++; }

Conditions, so you can weigh the numbers: .NET 10, Release build, 50M acquisitions per round, best-of-9 after a warmup, running in a small 2-core Linux container. That's not a lab bench and I'm not pretending it is. I care about the ratio between A, B and C on the same box in the same breath, not the absolute nanoseconds.

The numbers that didn't cooperate

First run:

[A: lock(object)     ] best= 822.6 ms   16.45 ns/op
[B: lock(Lock)       ] best= 882.4 ms   17.65 ns/op
[C: Lock.EnterScope()] best= 801.9 ms   16.04 ns/op
B vs A speedup: 0.93x

So the new type came out slower than the plain object. I ran it again figuring I'd caught a bad round:

[A: lock(object)     ] best= 927.8 ms   18.56 ns/op
[B: lock(Lock)       ] best= 802.9 ms   16.06 ns/op
B vs A speedup: 1.16x

Now Lock is ahead by 16%. Run it a third time and it's 1.12x. The honest read isn't "Lock is 0.93x" or "Lock is 1.16x" — it's that on this box, in the uncontended path, the two are a coin flip. Everything lands in the 16–18 ns/op band and the ordering swaps depending on which run I squint at. There is no free 2x here. There's barely a difference I'd stake a sentence on.

That's the part I want to be straight about, because it would've been easy to run until I got the 1.16x round and paste only that. The win I went looking for isn't in this benchmark.

So why switch, then?

Here's the turn, and it's why I still took the reviewer's advice. The reason to reach for Lock was never the raw speed of an uncontended acquire — it's that the type closes a door you didn't know was open. With lock(someObject) you can lock on anything: a string, a boxed value, a public field some other class can also see and lock on. Every one of those is a bug waiting for a bad day. With a Lock field, the type says exactly what it's for, and if you try to lock something that isn't a Lock the compiler's fine but you've clearly signaled intent. The bigger one for me: the analyzer now flags await inside a lock(Lock) scope, because you can't hold an EnterScope() across an await. The old pattern let that compile and then deadlock in production at 2am.

So the value is the stuff that doesn't show up on a stopwatch at all. Clearer ownership, a type that can't be misused as a public gate, a compiler that catches the await-inside-lock footgun. The performance is, at worst, a wash, and the design is better. That's a fine trade — I just can't sell it with the number I thought I'd have.

My honest opinion: migrate your locks to Lock as you touch the code, not in a big mechanical sweep. A dedicated Lock field is the better default for new code and I'd push back in review on a fresh lock(new object()). But if you're eyeing a repo-wide find-and-replace because someone told you it's faster, don't. You'll burn a day and a risky diff chasing a speedup that, uncontended, isn't there. And note what I did not test honestly: heavy multi-threaded contention is where Lock's design is actually supposed to pay off, and two cores in a container is the worst possible place to measure that. I'm not going to hand you a contention number I don't trust.

Here's the whole thing if you want to run it yourself — a net10.0 console app, dotnet run -c Release. Nudge Iterations and Rounds to fit your box:

using System.Diagnostics;

const int Iterations = 50_000_000;
const int Rounds = 9;

object _objectGate = new();
Lock _lockGate = new();
long counter = 0;

// warm up both paths before timing
RunObjectLock(1_000_000, ref counter);
RunTypedLock(1_000_000, ref counter);
RunTypedLockExplicit(1_000_000, ref counter);
counter = 0;

Console.WriteLine($"iterations per round: {Iterations:N0}, rounds: {Rounds}");
Console.WriteLine($"processor count: {Environment.ProcessorCount}\n");

var objectMs   = BestOf(Rounds, () => RunObjectLock(Iterations, ref counter));
var typedMs    = BestOf(Rounds, () => RunTypedLock(Iterations, ref counter));
var explicitMs = BestOf(Rounds, () => RunTypedLockExplicit(Iterations, ref counter));

Report("A: lock(object)     ", objectMs, Iterations);
Report("B: lock(Lock)       ", typedMs, Iterations);
Report("C: Lock.EnterScope()", explicitMs, Iterations);
Console.WriteLine($"\nB vs A speedup: {objectMs / typedMs:F2}x");

double RunObjectLock(int n, ref long c)
{
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) lock (_objectGate) { c++; }
    sw.Stop();
    return sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
}

double RunTypedLock(int n, ref long c)
{
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) lock (_lockGate) { c++; }
    sw.Stop();
    return sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
}

double RunTypedLockExplicit(int n, ref long c)
{
    var sw = Stopwatch.StartNew();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) using (_lockGate.EnterScope()) { c++; }
    sw.Stop();
    return sw.Elapsed.TotalMilliseconds;
}

static double BestOf(int rounds, Func<double> run)
{
    double best = double.MaxValue;
    for (int r = 0; r < rounds; r++) best = Math.Min(best, run());
    return best;
}

static void Report(string label, double ms, int iterations) =>
    Console.WriteLine($"[{label}] best={ms,7:F1} ms   {ms * 1_000_000.0 / iterations,5:F2} ns/op");

Have you swapped your locks over yet, and did you see anything on the clock, or was it a wash for you too? Curious whether a beefier box with real contention tells a different story.

— still benchmarking things nobody put on the sprint board

articles.title: Dukaan Munshi: the shop notebook that talks, and does the awkward “paise?” for you
articles.description: What I Built   Every neighbourhood shop in India runs on udhaar: Sharma ji takes ₹500 of...
articles.body_html:
What I Built

Every neighbourhood shop in India runs on udhaar: Sharma ji takes ₹500 of ration now and pays on the 1st. The record of it is a paper notebook or somebody's memory, and the hardest part isn't the writing. It's the asking. Nobody wants to be the one who says "bhaiya, paise?"

Dukaan Munshi (munshi means the shop's clerk) is a private khata that does both. The shopkeeper says or types what happened, in Hindi, Hinglish or English:

Sharma ji ne 500 udhaar liya, Gupta ji ne 200 diye

An open Gemma model running on the shop's own computer turns that into ledger entries and keeps every customer's balance. For anyone who owes money, it writes a WhatsApp reminder in the tone the shopkeeper picks: meethi (soft), seedhi (direct) or mazaakiya (a little funny, never shaming), in Hinglish, Hindi or English. One tap opens WhatsApp with the message ready to send.

Who would pay: a small shop that sells on credit and wants a smarter notebook that costs nothing every month and keeps its customer list at home.

Demo

Try it with nothing to install: https://abhyudaysharma.github.io/Dukaan-Munshi/

The online version runs in a simple mode (no Gemma), so you can see how it looks and feels. Press "demo khata" to load made-up customers. The smart reading and the nicer reminders come from Gemma on your own computer, with the three commands below.

📸

📸

To run it with Gemma (you need Node 18+ and Ollama):

bash
ollama pull gemma3:4b
git clone https://github.com/Abhyudaysharma/Dukaan-Munshi.git
cd Dukaan-Munshi && node server.js

Then open http://localhost:3000. There is nothing else to install.

Code

Abhyudaysharma / Munshi

Dukaan Munshi 📒

Bolo, munshi likh lega. A private khata (credit ledger) for small shops. Say what happened in Hindi, Hinglish or English ("Sharma ji ne 500 udhaar liya, Gupta ji ne 200 diye") and a Gemma model running on the shop's own machine turns it into ledger entries, keeps each customer's balance, and writes a polite WhatsApp reminder for anyone who owes money.

Try it with nothing installed: the live demo works in demo mode (simple rules instead of Gemma). Press "demo khata" to load made-up customers.

Why a shop would pay for it

Every kirana shop runs on udhaar, and the khata is usually a paper notebook or someone's memory. Chasing money is the awkward part. Munshi does the writing and the wording, in the shopkeeper's language, and the customer list never leaves the shop.

How it works

  • Capture: type or speak (browser voice typing, hi-IN). Munshi…
View on GitHub

How I Built It

The AI part is Gemma (gemma3:4b) running on the shop's own computer through Ollama. The app only ever talks to that local model, never to an online AI service.

A few choices I care about:

  1. You confirm before anything is saved. Money is the wrong place for a silent guess. After the shopkeeper speaks, Munshi shows what it understood (udhaar or jama, the name, the amount) in boxes they can fix. Nothing goes into the khata until they press save.

  2. The app doesn't blindly trust the model. Entries with an unknown type, a zero amount or no name are thrown away. Reminders are cleaned of stray symbols. The names already in the khata are given to the model, so "sharma" goes to the existing "Sharma ji" instead of creating a second customer.

  3. It still works with no model. If Gemma isn't running, a small set of simple rules reads plain notes, and ready-made messages cover the reminders. That's also what lets anyone try the online demo.

  4. Reminders that aren't rude. The model is told never to threaten, shame or invent dates, and to always use the exact amount, written the Indian way (₹12,34,567).

  5. The money maths is careful. ₹0.1 + ₹0.2 comes out as ₹0.3, cash sales never land on a customer, and someone who owes nothing can't be sent a reminder. I wrote a test suite for all of this, and I tried the full flow (speak, check, save, remind) in a real browser.

What's still rough

Gemma's Hindi at this small size is the weakest part, and the simple reader is deliberately basic. Voice typing depends on the browser. The khata lives in one browser, so there's no syncing between devices yet.

Why Does Open Innovation Matter?

A shop's customer list is private. Who owes whom, and how much, is exactly what a shopkeeper won't paste into someone else's cloud. Here the model, the app and the khata all stay on the shop's own computer.
It costs nothing to run. A shop on thin margins won't pay per message. A local model is free, so rewriting a reminder five times costs nothing.
No lock-in. I can swap Gemma for another open model, or change how the reminders sound, without waiting on anyone.
It can be made better for this job. Because the model is open, it can later be tuned on a region's Hindi and local item names.
It works with poor internet. The app opens without a connection, and nothing in the main flow needs an online service.

Where a closed model would honestly win: smoother Hindi and fewer misreadings of messy speech. For a khata, I'll take private, free and editable.

Prize Categories

Best Use of Gemma. Gemma runs on the shop's own computer and is the core of the app: it reads the shopkeeper's notes into entries and writes every reminder. The app checks everything it returns, and you can switch between Gemma versions.

Bolo, munshi likh lega. 📒

articles.title: I Replaced runc with a Rust Container Runtime (youki) for a Week
articles.description: The Boring Layer That Matters Most   Every container you've ever run — docker run...
articles.body_html:
The Boring Layer That Matters Most

Every container you've ever run — docker run hello-world included — went through a tiny binary called runc before it became a process. It creates the namespaces, sets up the cgroups, drops privileges, and hands off to your entrypoint.

You never think about it. And that's the problem.

runc is written in Go + C (yes, C — for the nsenter and pivot_root bits that Go can't handle cleanly). It's been the reference implementation since 2014. It's also the layer where CVE-2024-21626 (a container escape) lived.

What if that layer was memory-safe by construction?

Enter youki — a container runtime written entirely in Rust, now a CNCF Sandbox project.

What Is youki?

youki (Japanese for "container") is an OCI runtime-spec implementation in Rust. It's a drop-in replacement for runc: same CLI, same spec, same integration path through containerd, Podman, or Docker.

Fact Detail
Language Rust (pure, except a libseccomp-rs FFI shim being replaced)
CNCF status Sandbox (accepted Oct 17, 2024)
GitHub youki-dev/youki
Stars ~7,300
License Apache 2.0
Adopters Azure Kubernetes Service, Docker, containerd/runwasi
Contributing orgs Microsoft, Docker, Red Hat

The key differentiator vs. runc: no Go runtime startup, no C nsenter binary, no mixed-language memory safety boundary. The entire create → start → delete lifecycle lives in one Rust binary with compile-time safety guarantees.

The Benchmarks (Honest Version)

The headline number from youki's own repo:

Runtime Time (mean ± σ)        Range (min … max)    vs youki
youki   111.5 ms ± 11.6 ms     84.0 ms … 142.5 ms   100%
runc    224.6 ms ± 12.0 ms     190.5 ms … 255.4 ms  200%
crun     47.3 ms ±  2.8 ms     42.4 ms …  56.2 ms   42%

Youki is ~2× faster than runc for create → start → delete. But crun is ~2.5× faster than youki.

Here's the honest context:

Scenario Does it matter?
Single long-lived container No. 100ms of startup is noise over a 7-day uptime.
Serverless: 10k containers/min Yes. A 100ms savings × 10k = 1,000 CPU-seconds per minute reclaimed.
K8s pod churn (CI/CD, spot nodes) Moderately. Image pull + CNI + scheduling dominate; runtime is ~5–10% of total.
Edge/embedded (tight RAM) Yes. youki's binary is smaller and RSS is lower per instance.

The real win isn't raw speed — it's the Rust safety guarantee. You're not betting your node's security on a C memcpy in nsenter.

Setup: Replacing runc on a K8s Node

Prerequisites

  • Kubernetes 1.28+ with containerd (not Docker Engine)
  • Linux kernel 5.10+ (youki drops older kernel support to use modern features)
  • cargo / just for building from source (or use a pre-built binary)

Step 1: Build youki 

git clone https://github.com/youki-dev/youki.git
cd youki
just build
# Binary: ./target/release/youki

Or grab a release binary from GitHub Releases.

Step 2: Register with containerd

Edit /etc/containerd/config.toml (or use containerd config path):

[plugins."io.containerd.grpc.v1.cri".containerd.runtimes.youki]
  runtimeType = "io.containerd.youki.v1"

Then install the shim (youki ships a containerd-compatible shim):

sudo cp target/release/youki /usr/local/bin/
sudo cp target/release/containerd-shim-youki-v1 /usr/local/bin/

Restart containerd:

sudo systemctl restart containerd

Step 3: Create a RuntimeClass 

apiVersion: node.k8s.io/v1
kind: RuntimeClass
metadata:
  name: youki
handler: youki
scheduling:
  nodeSelector:
    kubernetes.io/arch: amd64

kubectl apply -f runtimeclass-youki.yaml

Step 4: Run a Pod with youki 

apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: youki-test
spec:
  runtimeClassName: youki
  containers:
  - name: app
    image: nginx:alpine
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "32Mi"
        cpu: "10m"

kubectl apply -f youki-pod.yaml
kubectl get pod youki-test -o wide
# youki-test   1/1   Running   0   2s

Verify it's actually using youki:

kubectl exec youki-test -- cat /proc/1/cgroup
# Confirms cgroup v2 hierarchy managed by youki

Step 5: Run It for a Week (What I Noticed)

I ran a 3-node k3s cluster with a mix of workloads:

  • 20 long-lived API pods (Go, ~50 MB each)
  • A CI pipeline spawning 50–200 short-lived pods/day
  • A cron job that scales a batch processor 0 → 10 → 0 every hour

What went well:

  1. Zero crashes, zero OOMs in the runtime itself. The Rust error handling is visible in logs — when something goes wrong, you get a structured Error with context, not a segfault.
  2. Short-lived pods were noticeably snappier. My CI pods (build → test → delete) came up ~30–50ms faster than runc. Not dramatic per-pod, but across 200 pods/day it added up.
  3. Rootless mode was cleaner. youki create with --rootless worked without the newuidmap/subuid gymnastics that runc sometimes needs.
  4. Binary size. youki: ~8 MB. runc: ~12 MB. crun: ~3 MB. On an edge node with 512 MB RAM, every MB counts.

What was rough:

  1. cgroups v1 support is there but v2 is the path of least resistance. If your distro still defaults to v1 (looking at you, CentOS 7), you'll hit edge cases.
  2. No --checkpoint/--restore (CRIU) yet. If you rely on live migration or pause/resume, you're stuck on runc.
  3. Docs are thin. The user docs cover the basics but there's no "migrating a production cluster from runc to youki" guide. You're on your own.
  4. One C dependency remains. libseccomp-rs is an FFI wrapper around the C libseccomp. The team is working on a pure-Rust replacement, but it's not done.

youki vs. runc vs. crun: Where Each Wins

Dimension runc crun youki
Language Go + C C Rust
Memory safety ❌ (C portion) ❌ ✅ (99% — one FFI shim)
Create→delete (benchmark) 224 ms 47 ms 111 ms
Binary size ~12 MB ~3 MB ~8 MB
cgroups v2 ✅ ✅ ✅
Rootless ✅ ✅ ✅ (cleanest)
CRIU (checkpoint/restore) ✅ ✅ ❌ (roadmap)
Wasm support ❌ ❌ ✅ (first-class)
CNCF governance ❌ (OCI) ✅ (Sandbox) ✅ (Sandbox)
Production battle-testing 10+ years 5+ years ~3 years
Best for Default, compatibility Max performance, minimal footprint Safety + Wasm + future-proofing

The honest takeaway: If you need maximum raw speed today, crun wins. If you need the safest runtime with a path to Wasm workloads, youki is the pick. runc remains the "it just works" default.

The Wasm Angle (Why This Matters More Than You Think)

Here's the part that excites me: youki is the low-level runtime that powers runwasi (the containerd shim for Wasm workloads) and, by extension, SpinKube.

The architecture:

containerd
  └── containerd-shim-runwasi (Rust)
        └── youki libcontainer (Rust) ← shared library
              └── Wasmtime / Wasmer / WasmEdge

Youki's libcontainer crate is used as a library by other Rust container tools. That means the same memory-safe, OCI-compliant primitives that run your nginx:alpine pod also run your Wasm modules. One codebase, two workload types, same security guarantees.

This is the "Rust container stack" taking shape:

Layer Rust project Role
Runtime youki OCI container lifecycle
Shim runwasi Wasm on containerd
Orchestrator SpinKube Wasm on Kubernetes
Image tooling naftiko Build OCI/Wasm images
Spec oci-spec (Rust crate) The spec itself, in Rust

Youki is the foundation. If it's not solid, nothing above it is.

What's Missing (and Where Funding Helps)

youki is in CNCF Sandbox — the earliest maturity level. The project is healthy (active commits, 80+ contributors, backing from Microsoft/Docker/Red Hat) but under-resourced for what it needs to do:

  • Pure-Rust seccomp (eliminate the last C dependency) — significant engineering effort
  • SELinux in Rust — needed for RHEL/CentOS production adoption
  • CRIU support — checkpoint/restore is table-stakes for production
  • OCI conformance test suite — a dedicated, automated compliance harness
  • Docs and migration guides — "how do I move a 500-node cluster from runc to youki?"
  • Security audit — a formal audit would be a major trust signal for enterprise adoption
  • Conference presence — KubeCon, RustConf, containersc — the project needs more visibility

No LFX Crowdfunding campaign is active yet. If you use or evaluate youki, the highest-impact things you can do:

  1. Contribute — even docs, test cases, or bug reports. GitHub
  2. Run it in production and report what breaks (or doesn't)
  3. Write about it — this article is a start, but we need more "I ran youki in a real cluster" content
  4. Watch for an LFX Crowdfunding launch — CNCF funding page

TL;DR

Question Answer
Is youki production-ready? For new, non-critical workloads: yes. For a 500-node cluster: not yet.
Is it faster than runc? ~2× for create/delete. Yes, but crun is faster still.
Is it safer than runc? Yes — memory-safe Rust eliminates the C nsenter attack surface.
Should I switch today? If you're running Wasm workloads or want to be early on the Rust container stack: yes. Otherwise: watch this space.
What's the risk? It's a Sandbox project. The API could shift. CRIU is missing. Docs are thin.

Final Thought

The container runtime is the most underappreciated layer in the stack. It's the thing that's always running, that touches every syscall, that sits between your workload and the kernel. For a decade, that layer was a Go binary with a C sidecar.

Now there's a Rust option with CNCF governance, major-company backing, and a clear path to being the foundation for the next generation of container workloads (including Wasm).

I ran it for a week. It didn't break. It was faster. And the Rust error messages in the logs were genuinely pleasant to read.

That's about as good as "boring infrastructure" gets.

Have you tried youki in production? What broke? What didn't? Drop your experience in the comments — I'm especially curious about anyone running it alongside runwasi or SpinKube.

If you want to support the project, the best things right now are **contributing code/docs* and writing about your experience. The CNCF funding infrastructure is ready when the project is.*
